title: A daily hukamnama
hookLine: a verse-of-the-day app picks for you; a hukamnama is the hymn nobody picks
tomorrow: what if you read the whole Granth, slowly, your own way?
last: THE TRANSLATION IS NOT THE GURU.

lines: VERSE OF THE DAY: SOMEONE PICKED.
cards: A notification lights up the phone before sunrise: verse of the day. Somebody, somewhere, picked it. Now a different early morning.
A cloth is lifted, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened, and nobody picks. The hymn at the top of the left-hand page is read out, and that's the answer to yesterday's question. Who chooses the page?
No one. That hymn is the hukamnama: today's order. At Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar it's taken each morning and shared, so a grandmother in California can hear the same hymn before breakfast.

teach.b: Hukam means order, command. You met it before as the order the whole world runs by. The hukamnama is that order made small enough to hold: one hymn for one day.
The Sikh code describes how it's taken.
Open the Granth, read the hymn that begins at the top of the left-hand page. If it started on the page before, turn back and read it from its beginning. Hear how physical that is.
The weight of the cloth. The sound of a page turning in a quiet room. Your eyes going to the top left, not wandering down to find a line you like better.
Taking the hukam is a way of saying: not my pick today. Now the misunderstanding worth clearing up.
It doesn't say what will happen by evening. It's a teaching to live by, the Guru's word for this day, and it might be about humility on a day you wanted comfort.
Something to tell someone tonight: in gurdwaras, the day's guidance is read from a hymn nobody chose, and whole families far apart can start the morning on the same words.

how: Each morning a hukamnama is taken at Harmandir Sahib and in gurdwaras by opening the Guru Granth Sahib and reading the hymn at the top of the left-hand page; many Sikhs read the day's hukamnama from Harmandir Sahib online or in an app.

games.q: you open the Granth for the morning's hukam. the hymn at the top of the left page began on the page before. what do you do?
o: read only what's on the left page; that part is the hukam.
pick a hymn further down that fits the day you're having.
turn back and read the hymn from its beginning.
games.why: the code says to read the hymn whole: if it began on the earlier page, turn back to its start. and no picking a nicer one: not my pick today.

practice: Open today's hukamnama, in an app or online, or open a gutka with both hands and feel the page turn. Rest one hand flat on your chest and read the hymn's first lines aloud, slowly, feeling the sound move under your palm.
Then stay with the breath, and let one phrase from it be the one you keep.

wordCard.voice: A daily hukamnama: the hymn read each morning from the top of the Granth's left-hand page, taken as the Guru's order for the day. The thirteenth word of the year.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: hukamnama, the order: the hymn read as the Guru's word for the day.

carryVoice: Keep this: today's order, a hymn nobody picked, given to you for one day. Thirteen of twenty, opened.
